content: Adolescent adherence counseling sessions are most frequently conducted by counselors, doctors/clinicians, nurses, and caregivers. Less commonly, these sessions involve community health workers, pharmacists or pharmacy technicians, psychologists, social workers, and peer supporters. Many facilities reported the absence of established guidelines or protocols for managing adolescents facing adherence challenges. Where such guidelines exist, recommended interventions include adherence counseling, caregiver engagement, treatment support, general counseling, peer support, activities and clubs, and home visits. Additional strategies mentioned include disclosure support, engagement with community health workers or community-based organizations (CBOs), increased clinic visit frequency, pill counts, and adopting a multidisciplinary approach to adolescent care. When defining treatment failure, many clinics provided criteria based on their practices. However, 45% of facilities lacked a clear determination of adherence. Pill counting was the most common method used (42%), followed by tracking pharmacy refills (11%), patient self-reports (9%), and viral suppression monitoring (4%). Some facilities combined these methods. Viral load monitoring was available in 60% of facilities, with routine testing conducted every six months or more frequently in most cases. Some facilities only performed viral load testing when treatment failure was suspected, often due to the lack of in-house viral load testing equipment. Regarding loss to follow-up (LTFU), only 4% of facilities lacked a clear definition. The most common definition was the absence of a clinic visit for three or more months (66%), followed by missing two or more consecutive visits (15%). Interventions for adolescents identified as LTFU included home visits (76%), telephone calls (50%), and engagement with community health workers or CBOs (30%). Less common methods included SMS, email, and school visits. Retention support services for adolescents were offered by 61% of facilities, with peer support, activities, and clubs (34%) and home visits (31%) being the most common approaches. Other strategies included general counseling, adherence counseling, caregiver engagement, nutritional support, and educational support. Facilities in East Africa were most likely to offer retention services (82%), followed by Southern Africa (64%) and West/Central Africa (31%). Adolescent-specific service delivery models varied. Thirty-five percent of facilities attended to adolescents separately from adults and children, while 31% combined services for all age groups. In East Africa, 56% of facilities adopted adolescent-specific service models, compared to 35% in Southern Africa and 7% in West/Central Africa. The most common feature of adolescent-specific services was the allocation of a dedicated clinic day or time (88%), followed by dedicated clinic staff (10%) and dedicated clinic spaces (8%). Transitioning from pediatric to adult services occurred at varying ages, with the most common being 18 years (23%), followed by 10 years (14%), 12 years (12%), 15 years (12%), and 20 or 21 years (7% each). Just over half of the facilities had guidelines in place to guide the transition process. Counseling to aid in the transition was provided by 63% of facilities, typically over three sessions lasting more than 15 minutes each. These sessions focused on the transition process, adherence, HIV disease management, emotional well-being, and other relevant topics. Pregnant adolescents were often transitioned to adult services earlier than standard procedures due to their pregnancy. This version maintains the detailed content while presenting it in a clear and professional manner suitable for medical experts.
